notes.meaning: God kept His word. Through Jeremiah He had promised that the exile in Babylon would last seventy years, and now that time was up. So the LORD moved the heart of Cyrus, the Persian king who had just conquered Babylon. The hearts of kings are in God's hand, and any good they do comes from Him stirring them to do it.

Cyrus gives the God of heaven the credit for his huge empire. He says God has given him a job: to build Him a house, meaning the temple, in Jerusalem. Many older writers think Cyrus had been shown Isaiah's prophecy, which named him long before he was born (Isaiah 44:28). Daniel may have been the one who showed it to him. Cyrus also had a habit of helping other peoples rebuild their shrines, as his own writings show.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the Jewish writer put Cyrus's decree into Israel's own words. On this view, Cyrus may have thanked his own Persian god, and the writer wrote that as "the LORD."

notes.meaning: Cyrus opens the door to any of God's people who want to go home. He blesses them ("may his God be with him") and tells them to go and rebuild the LORD's temple. No one was forced to go. Matthew Henry notes that Cyrus did not tell them to build a temple for Persia's gods. He let them worship the God of Israel alone.

The "survivors" are God's people still living in exile. Their neighbors were to help them with money, goods and animals, especially those too poor to make the trip. On top of this came "freewill offerings," gifts given gladly rather than demanded, for God's house. From the start, the goal was worship, not just moving back home.

The family leaders of Judah and Benjamin, along with the priests and Levites (the temple helpers), led the way. With them went everyone whose spirit God had stirred. The trip was long and risky, and Jerusalem lay in ruins, so many chose to stay in their comfortable homes. Matthew Henry sees a picture of the gospel here. Christ offers freedom from sin to all, and those who answer are the ones God's grace has made willing.

Their neighbors helped them with silver, gold, goods, animals and other valuables. Some of these helpers were non-Jews, and some were fellow Jews who stayed behind. God can turn the hearts of strangers to be kind to His people. Matthew Henry compares this to Israel leaving Egypt with gifts from the Egyptians.

Cyrus also gave back the temple's sacred dishes and tools. Nebuchadnezzar had carried them off and put them in the temple of his gods. Second Kings says they were "cut in pieces," but the word may only mean they were cut off from temple use. Matthew Henry sees God's care in keeping them safe, just as He keeps safe those who belong to Him.

The royal treasurer, Mithredath, counted the items out to Sheshbazzar, "the prince of Judah." Most of these commentaries think Sheshbazzar was the Babylonian court name of Zerubbabel, who was from King David's family line. Daniel and his friends were given new names in the same way. So leadership still stayed in David's house.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel were two different men. Sheshbazzar may have been an official who led the first stage, or even a Persian sent by Cyrus. Others note that neither view is free of problems.

notes.meaning: Here is the list of dishes, bowls and other items. The Geneva Notes say the "utensils" (older Bibles say "knives") were used for animal sacrifices, though the meaning of that word is not certain. The careful count shows how precious these things were, since people count treasures, not pebbles. Some great items, like the ark, are missing and were likely lost when the temple was destroyed.

The total was 5,400 gold and silver items, and Sheshbazzar brought them as the exiles went up to Jerusalem. The items listed add up to only 2,499. Some older writers think only the larger pieces were listed. Others think a number was miscopied over time. This was the first group home, and later groups came with Ezra and Nehemiah.
